titre: Ronan Point, 1968: a stove brings down a whole corner of the tower
accroche: On May 16, 1968, a resident lights her gas stove on the 18th floor of a London tower. The blast brings an entire corner down to the ground.
contenu_vulgarise:
On May 16, 1968, around 5:45 a.m., Ivy Hodge, a resident of Flat 90 on the 18th floor of the Ronan Point tower in Canning Town, in East London, strikes a match for her gas stove. A leak, caused by a cracked nut that was probably overtightened during installation, has filled the room with gas overnight. The explosion blows out the load-bearing wall of her living room. Completed two months earlier, the 22-story tower had been put up using the Danish Larsen & Nielsen system: large concrete panels cast in a factory, delivered to the site and simply bolted to one another, a fast construction method designed to meet the demand for social housing of the 1960s cheaply.

## A collapse that has nothing to do with a bomb

The blast itself is in fact modest: it destroys only one wall. But in this system, each panel stands only when supported by the one below it: nothing ties the floors to one another beyond that bolting. Deprived of support, the 19th-floor slabs fall onto those of the 18th, which fall in turn onto those of the 17th, and so on down to the ground floor: an entire corner of the building, from roof to ground, collapses in a cascade. Four people die, seventeen are injured. The public inquiry, led by the jurist Hugh Griffiths at the government's request, concludes that the tower met the regulations in force, and that it is precisely those regulations that are at fault: nothing required that a wall be able to give way without taking down everything it supported.

## What the 1986 demolition reveals

The UK National Archives hold the file of this inquiry, conducted from June 8 to August 20, 1968. Its conclusions are not about gas stoves, but about a notion until then absent from the regulations: a local failure must never lead to a collapse disproportionate to its cause. The fifth amendment to the British Building Regulations, as early as 1970, makes it a formal requirement (today Part A of the English building code) and requires new towers to withstand a given explosive force, whatever its origin. Ronan Point itself is strengthened and remains inhabited, until architect Sam Webb, a witness at the 1968 inquiry, secures its evacuation in 1984. The tower is demolished methodically in 1986: the demolition crews then discover bolts missing at many joints, and holes meant to be filled with concrete stuffed with debris and old newspapers. The 1968 failure had revealed nothing exceptional; it had only shown, once and for all, what fast and poorly supervised construction could hide behind a wall.

repere.texte: The Ronan Point explosion does not kill or injure through its blast, which destroys only one wall: it is the stacked slabs of the upper floors that kill four people and injure seventeen as they collapse in a cascade to the ground.

carte.punch: A stove explosion changed building rules around the world.
carte.idee: On May 16, 1968, a gas leak blows up an apartment in the Ronan Point tower in London. The blast, modest, destroys only one wall, but the upper slabs collapse in a cascade. The inquiry establishes that no building may collapse disproportionately to its cause.

quiz.question: Why did the 1968 collapse of Ronan Point change building regulations in several countries?
choix: Because the inquiry revealed that the gas stove involved had been defective from manufacture
Because the inquiry showed that no rule prevented a local failure from bringing down an entire corner of the building
Because the prefabricated concrete used for the tower proved to be below standard quality
Because residents had received no safety instructions in case of a gas leak
quiz.explication: The inquiry concludes that the tower met the regulations of the time: it is those regulations, which guaranteed no resistance to disproportionate collapse, that are at fault, not a manufacturing defect in the stove, nor the quality of the concrete, nor the absence of instructions, none of which the inquiry upholds.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What was the immediate cause of the May 16, 1968 explosion at Ronan Point?
choix: A gas leak from a cracked nut, probably overtightened when the stove was installed
A short circuit in the 18th-floor electrical panel
A leak from the building's communal boiler
A flaw in the prefabricated concrete panels themselves
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The leak came from a cracked nut connecting the stove to the gas line, probably overtightened during installation; neither the electrical system, nor a communal boiler, nor a flaw in the concrete panels was behind the explosion itself.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What did the Ronan Point demolition crews discover in 1986?
choix: That many joints between panels lacked their bolts, and that holes meant to be filled with concrete contained debris and old newspapers
That the tower had actually been built two stories taller than planned
That the concrete panels came from another site and had never been tested
That the building rested on foundations that were not deep enough
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The demolition reveals bolts missing at several joints and holes filled with debris and newspapers instead of concrete; nothing indicates an altered height, untested panels brought in from elsewhere, or foundations that were too shallow.
